title: mozilla-ai/otari — Open-source, OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway you run yourself. One endpoint for 40+ providers, with virtual keys, budgets, and usage tracking.
content:
An OpenAI-compatible LLM gateway you own and run.
Route one endpoint to 40+ providers, issue virtual keys, enforce budgets, and track usage.
Docs · otari.ai · Launch blog · Discord
Otari sits between your applications and model providers. It authenticates requests, resolves provider credentials, enforces budgets before dispatch, and records usage afterwards. Provider calls go through any-llm.
Run Otari standalone with your own database and provider keys, or connect a data plane to otari.ai.
- One OpenAI and Anthropic-compatible endpoint for many providers
- Provider credentials stay behind the gateway
- Revocable API keys with user, workspace, and model scope
- Budget checks before spend and usage records after settlement
- Local routing policies for failover, weighting, and learned selection
- Optional code execution, web search, MCP, inference guardrails, and file understanding
Run an ephemeral standalone gateway with Docker:
docker run --rm -p 8000:8000 \
  -e OTARI_MASTER_KEY=SET_A_MASTER_KEY \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY=YOUR_OPENAI_KEY \
  -e OTARI_CONFIG_YAML='
default_pricing: true
providers:
  openai:
    api_key: ${OPENAI_API_KEY}
' \
  mzdotai/otari:latest \
  otari serve
On the first empty database, Otari creates an API key and prints it once:
No API keys found. Created bootstrap key for first run. Save this key now:
tk-...
Send a request with that key:
curl http://localhost:8000/api/v1/chat/completions \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer tk-..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
    "model": "openai:gpt-4o-mini",
    "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello."}]
  }'
OpenAI clients work by setting base_url to
http://localhost:8000/api/v1.
This container uses SQLite inside the container and is deleted when it stops. Use the Compose setup below for persistent data.
The command a developer runs next to a coding agent (otari hook,
otari import claude-code) installs on its own, without the server:
brew install mozilla-ai/tap/otari
See Agent Guardrails and Use with Claude Code.
git clone https://github.com/mozilla-ai/otari
cd otari
cp config.example.yml config.yml
# Set a master key, provider credentials, and pricing in config.yml.
# Provider copies of attached files need a pepper of their own. Compose reads .env.
grep -qs OTARI_PROVIDER_ACCOUNT_PEPPER .env || echo "OTARI_PROVIDER_ACCOUNT_PEPPER=$(openssl rand -base64 32)" >> .env
docker compose pull
docker compose up -d
Compose runs Otari with PostgreSQL. Optional profiles add the code sandbox, web search, and guardrail services:
docker compose --profile code-exec --profile web-search --profile guardrails up -d
The dashboard is served at http://localhost:8000/. To store provider keys
through the dashboard, set OTARI_SECRET_KEY to a Fernet key generated by
otari gen-secret-key.
A one-click deployment template is available for Railway.
When OTARI_MODE is unset, OTARI_AI_TOKEN selects hybrid mode; otherwise
Otari defaults to standalone. A mode says what a process serves, not who runs it,
so "hosted" is not the opposite of "self-hosted". See
Runtime modes.
The core completion routes are:
- POST /api/v1/chat/completions
- POST /api/v1/messages
- POST /api/v1/responses
Standalone also serves the broader OpenAI-compatible and management APIs. The
running server publishes Swagger UI at /api/v1/docs and OpenAPI at
/api/v1/openapi.json. See API reference.
The dashboard manages providers, models, routing, tools, keys, members, budgets, settings, activity, and usage. Its navigation adapts to the deployment mode and the signed-in person's authority. See Admin dashboard.
git clone https://github.com/mozilla-ai/otari
cd otari
uv sync --dev
cp config.example.yml config.yml
uv run otari serve --config config.yml
For local development without PostgreSQL, change database_url to
sqlite+aiosqlite:///./otari.db.
Common checks:
make test
make lint
make typecheck
See CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a pull request.
Apache 2.0. See LICENSE.

report.summary: Mozilla AI's Otari is an open-source, self-hosted gateway that gives teams one OpenAI-compatible endpoint to 40+ LLM providers with keys, budgets, and usage tracking.
report.background: Enterprises and developers increasingly route work across multiple LLM providers—OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and open-weight hosts—to optimize cost, latency, and capability. But each provider has its own API, credentials, pricing, and rate limits, so teams duplicate integration code and scatter secrets across applications. A gateway layer centralizes this: one API surface, credentials held server-side, and policy enforced in one place. The category has grown quickly, with hosted routers like OpenRouter and open-source proxies like LiteLLM. Mozilla AI, which has built open-source AI tooling including the any-llm abstraction library, positions Otari as a self-owned alternative that keeps provider credentials and usage data inside the operator's infrastructure. The timing reflects cost pressure on AI budgets and a push for vendor-neutral, auditable infrastructure as LLM usage moves from prototypes into production.
key_points: A single OpenAI- and Anthropic-compatible endpoint routes to 40+ providers through any-llm, so existing OpenAI SDK clients only need their base_url changed. Provider credentials stay behind the gateway rather than being distributed to every application.

Virtual API keys can be issued, scoped to users, workspaces, and models, and revoked. Budgets are checked before a request is dispatched, and usage is recorded after settlement, giving operators spend control and per-key accountability.

Local routing policies support failover, weighted distribution, and learned selection across providers, so teams can shift traffic during an outage or rebalance for cost and latency without changing application code. Policies are evaluated inside the gateway, close to credentials and budgets.

Deployment is flexible: an ephemeral Docker container with SQLite for trials, Docker Compose with PostgreSQL for persistence, a dashboard, Swagger/OpenAPI docs, and a Railway template. Optional profiles add code execution, web search, MCP, guardrails, and file understanding.

It is Apache 2.0 licensed and includes a CLI hook for coding agents (otari hook, otari import claude-code) that installs without the server, plus a hybrid mode that can connect a local data plane to otari.ai, giving teams a path from solo setups to a managed control plane.
report.impact: Otari signals that the LLM gateway is becoming the control plane for AI applications, not just a convenience proxy. For the industry, it adds a credible open-source, Mozilla-backed option to a field led by LiteLLM, OpenRouter, and commercial gateways, and it pushes provider routing, budgets, and key management toward commodity infrastructure. For developers, it cuts integration work and makes multi-model experimentation safer, but self-hosting brings operational duties: database backups, upgrades, secret management, and latency overhead. For regular users, the benefits are indirect but real—apps can fail over more gracefully, teams can cap runaway AI spend, and sensitive prompts and provider keys stay inside the operator's infrastructure rather than a third-party router.
report.tools: To compare approaches, look at LiteLLM (open-source OpenAI-compatible proxy with budgets and routing), OpenRouter (hosted multi-provider router), Portkey's gateway, and Cloudflare AI Gateway. Otari builds on Mozilla's any-llm library, which is worth watching for provider abstraction. For observability alongside a gateway, pair it with Langfuse or Helicone. Start with the Docker one-liner and the Swagger UI at /api/v1/docs.
